Indian School of Business · Software Product Management

Pratisad Charge Networks: Four Hundred and Ten First Tries

The company is fictional; the market and the named brands are real.

1. Baner, Pune — Sunday, 15 November 2026, 11.40 p.m.

Bhanuja Indulkar could not bring herself to change the slide title. It said Self-service swap: ready to scale. Ten hours from now she would ask the board of Pratisad Charge Networks Private Limited to release ₹32.88 crore for twelve hundred self-service battery-swap cabinets — or not ask, and explain why she had changed her mind.

Three printouts lay beside the laptop. The June lab study in Pune: twelve riders, five tasks, fifty-five of sixty attempts successful, 92 per cent, the number that had travelled through the company all summer. The August field study Bandita Inarkar ran in Nashik and Nagpur: thirty-one riders, no moderator, sixteen of the thirty-one finishing a swap, 52 per cent. And September telemetry from the fourteen pilot kiosks, where 8,111 of 9,480 started sessions completed — 85.6 per cent.

Three studies of one cabinet, and nobody could say which described the product she proposed to build. Barkha Irsalkar, in Berlin, called June a test of a prototype no rider would ever meet, because the moderator had been allowed to speak. Bibek Indurkar, in Toronto, answered with a composite he called the Swap Readiness Index, 87.7 per cent. What Indulkar kept returning to was in none of the summaries: in September, 410 riders had walked up to one of the five unattended kiosks for the first time in their lives.

2. The company, and a decision made in March 2024

Pratisad was founded in Pune in 2022 by Baliram Indapurkar, formerly of a two-wheeler component maker in Chakan. The thesis was narrow: the constraint on electric two- and three-wheelers was not the vehicle but the eight minutes a gig rider could not spare.

By March 2024 the company had a working cabinet and no money for a second tooling cycle. On Monday 11 March 2024 Indapurkar signed an agreement with Pargati Enclosures Private Limited of Chakan that froze the cabinet's external geometry for a unit price the company could survive. Three dimensions in that drawing have governed every argument since: a seven-inch, 400-nit panel recessed 110 mm behind the bay door; the panel centre 1,430 mm above ground; and eight bays in a two-by-four array with no illuminated indicator, because the cabinet was always to be worked by an attendant.

The network was built on attendants. A ₹386 crore Series B in January 2025 paid for 212 attended points by October 2025 and 318 across six cities by September 2026. Attendants were also why contribution per point never approached plan, so in March 2026 the board approved self-service on the frozen enclosure. An addendum that month set ₹2.74 lakh a cabinet against a commitment to 1,200 units by 31 March 2027, with a ₹4.6 crore shortfall fee.

3. The industry

By late 2026 the Indian charging market had split into three businesses that only looked like one. Ather Energy and Ola Electric sold vehicles and treated charging as a vehicle feature. Tata Power, Jio-bp and Statiq sold kilowatt-hours to four-wheeler owners content to wait. The swap business — Battery Smart, Sun Mobility, Zypp and Pratisad — sold time, and competed on whether a rider believed a charged battery would be waiting.

Demand came from gig fleets: riders working for Zepto, Swiggy, Zomato and Blinkit were three-quarters of September volume. None was Pratisad's customer contractually — individuals paying per swap over NPCI rails through PhonePe or Paytm, free to walk to a competitor's cabinet.

Regulation bore on the product in three places. The Bureau of Indian Standards' light electric vehicle charging specification, IS 17017-2-6, governed the connector and electrical safety — what the 2024 drawing had frozen. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed rider telemetry. GST and Maharashtra's EV policy incentives decided whether a marginal site contributed at all. Abroad, Behram Ichalkar had sold twelve cabinets to Payaam Mobility FZ-LLC in Dubai, a last-mile operator running 900 electric two-wheelers, with an option on sixty more contingent on a self-service release by early 2027. Payaam's depots are gated and staffed.

4. The situation in detail

The programme ran three studies in five months, each designed in ignorance of what the next would find.

Round 1, Pune, June 2026. Irsalkar flew in from Berlin with a clickable prototype of the kiosk flow on a spare seven-inch panel bolted to a cabinet in the Hadapsar workshop. Twelve riders attempted five tasks each, with a moderator who could prompt once per task. Of sixty attempts, forty-five succeeded unassisted, ten after a prompt and five failed (Exhibit 2). The programme review was told 92 per cent.

Round 2, Nashik and Nagpur, August 2026. Inarkar ran the same five tasks on two real cabinets with the late-July build, unmoderated, five-minute cap, nobody to ask. A rider who failed a task did not reach the next, so denominators fall as the funnel narrows (Exhibit 3). Sixteen of thirty-one completed a swap end to end: 52 per cent.

The 92 and the 52 were argued over for three weeks before anyone wrote down that they were not the same measure. It was Irsalkar who extracted from Round 1 the comparable figure: five of the twelve Pune participants had cleared all five tasks unprompted, 42 per cent. On the point estimates, that measure put the unmoderated field study ahead of the lab.

The pilot, September 2026. Fourteen cabinets were converted, nine in Pune and five in Nashik. Nine kept their day-shift attendant, because those sites were already staffed and Indapurkar would not pull people before the festive peak; five had nobody. Completion across all fourteen was 85.6 per cent, and for ten days in October that number ended the argument.

What it concealed is in Exhibit 4. The nine attended kiosks completed 90.0 per cent of sessions, the five unattended 75.4 per cent, and within the unattended five, 410 sessions were a rider's first-ever attempt, of which 238 completed — 58 per cent. Neither the June lab, indoors, nor the August study under monsoon cloud had put a rider in front of that recessed 400-nit panel in direct sun. Fourteen of the forty-eight riders interviewed in October named it (Exhibit 6).

5. The people

Bhanuja Indulkar, vice-president, product, Pune, owns the recommendation. Position: software fixes, not a hardware retreat. Incentive: the addendum rests on her business case. Unsaid: she doubts any study tested whether a rider would choose a cabinet over charging at home.

Baliram Indapurkar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: the pilot is the only real test, because real riders paid real money. Incentive: a Series C that cannot survive a twenty-two-week delay. Unsaid: he has told two investors the cabinet works, citing 85.6 per cent.

Barkha Irsalkar, principal designer, Berlin. Position: June is worthless because a moderator spoke, the honest number is 42 per cent, and bay identification is a hardware defect. Incentive: she lost the 2024 geometry argument. Unsaid: her redesigned bay screen was in the build Inarkar tested, and task 2 was still the worst.

Bibek Indurkar, staff data scientist, Toronto. Position: weighted properly, the field data gives a Swap Readiness Index of 87.7 per cent, and 52 per cent is an artefact of a tiny sample. Incentive: the index is his instrument. Unsaid: it is the mean of the five task rates in Exhibit 3, each computed only over riders who got that far.

Bhavesh Ingle, vice-president, engineering, Bengaluru. Position: ship the fixes and let telemetry settle it at scale. Incentive: his 2027 roadmap is committed to fleet APIs for Payaam. Unsaid: the payment time-out in Exhibit 6 is a known UPI retry defect shelved in July.

Bhadra Itolikar, head of customer success, Singapore; her team made the October calls. Position: a software and signage problem, because only one reason in five was about hardware. Incentive: a desk already absorbing the night load. Unsaid: they closed the sheet at forty-eight completed interviews, not at a planned sample.

Behram Ichalkar, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: Payaam's depot has run cabinets since July without incident, so usability is settled and Pratisad should sell to fleets. Incentive: the sixty-cabinet option and his quota. Unsaid: at Payaam a technician does the swap while the rider waits outside the cage.

Bandita Inarkar, city operations lead, Nagpur, who ran Round 2. Position: riders can learn the cabinet, but not in the three minutes between deliveries. Incentive: she is judged on points live per month. Unsaid: she chose her two Round 2 cabinets because they were the two she could spare, both on quiet streets, one with a spotlight above it.

6. Voices

“Ninety-two per cent is not a number about our product. It is a number about a product that comes with a woman from Berlin standing next to it. Take her away and it is forty-two.”

Barkha Irsalkar, programme review, 24 August 2026

“Then explain Nashik. No moderator, no prompts, and fifty-two per cent finished. If removing the moderator costs fifty points, how did the unmoderated study beat the lab's own unassisted number?”

Bibek Indurkar, same thread

“Both of you are reading study design. I am reading September. Nine thousand four hundred and eighty sessions, eighty-five point six per cent completed, money in the bank.”

Baliram Indapurkar, management call, 9.00 p.m. IST, 13 November 2026 — 4.30 p.m. in Berlin, 10.30 a.m. in Toronto

“Sir, nine of those fourteen had someone standing there. Take the first-timers at the five that did not, and it is fifty-eight per cent.”

Bandita Inarkar, same call

“Eighteen of the eighty-six reasons riders gave us were about the battery not seating. One in five. The rest is screens, signage and a time-out — things we can ship on a Thursday.”

Bhadra Itolikar, customer success summary, 14 October 2026

“Dubai has done eleven thousand swaps since July with zero usability tickets. Where is this risk in the only site making money?”

Behram Ichalkar, email to Indapurkar, 10 November 2026

“Nobody has tested the bay being empty. Not in June, not in August. The flow we tested assumes a charged battery is waiting. Eight of forty-eight riders told us in October that it was not.”

Barkha Irsalkar, chat to Indulkar, 6.14 p.m. IST, 15 November 2026

7. The options as Indulkar sees them

A. Scale the software. Take all 1,200 cabinets on the frozen geometry; ship the bay-selection redesign, a sunlight mode and a UPI retry fix. Meets the March commitment, avoids the shortfall fee, allows the Maharashtra bid. Treats 58 per cent as a learning curve signage can shorten.

B. Hybrid by footfall. Self-service everywhere, attendants kept at the 420 highest-footfall sites: ₹1.03 crore a month in wages, ₹12.35 crore a year, and a concession that the product does not work unaided where it matters most.

C. A third round, with a retrofit. A bolt-on sun hood and an illuminated bay-indicator strip, leaving the frozen geometry untouched, at ₹9,400 a cabinet — ₹1.13 crore across 1,200 units — tested on first-time riders at unattended sites in the December sun. Six weeks of fieldwork, which means no firm schedule to Pargati by 30 November and so no delivery by 31 March.

D. Sell to fleets. Gated depots staffed by the client, where the rider never touches the panel. Payaam's option and two Indian prospects could absorb 340 cabinets. It also means telling a board that funded a street network that the street is the problem.

Indulkar has twice typed a line below the four and deleted it: none of these is a test of whether riders want this. Every option argues about whether a rider can work the cabinet. The Series B was raised on the claim that a rider would pay ₹96 to save eight minutes, and the group whose behaviour speaks to that — the 172 first-timers who walked away, averaging 4.1 further swaps against the completers' 9.4 — has been asked about nothing but the cabinet.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10.00 a.m. on Monday 16 November 2026 in Pune, and the decision cannot slide: Pargati needs a firm schedule by 30 November to deliver 1,200 cabinets by 31 March 2027, and the Maharashtra tender, which requires a committed 300 self-service points, closes that same day.

Money: ₹182 crore of cash and equivalents at 30 September 2026 against net burn of ₹9.4 crore a month in the September quarter — a little over nineteen months of runway from 1 October 2026. The cabinet order is ₹32.88 crore; the shortfall fee ₹4.6 crore; new tooling ₹7.4 crore and twenty-two weeks, which cannot be finished before March.

People: Irsalkar is the only designer who has run a session with a rider, and her Berlin contract ends in February 2027; Inarkar's team of nine is the only field research capacity and also runs 71 live points. Regulation: the DPDP consent notice does not cover product research, so the September logs cannot go into an external deck, and any retrofit touching the bay door re-opens the conformity file.

9. Sunday night

At 12.20 a.m. Indulkar filtered the September log again: unattended kiosks, first-ever session. Four hundred and ten rows. Two hundred and thirty-eight ended in a completed swap and 172 did not, and she could not decide whether that was a usability number, a value number, or a number about nine attendants she had not been allowed to move. She opened a message to Irsalkar, typed if we had one more week, what exactly would you put in front of a rider, and left it unsent.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of the three studies measure? State the denominator and the window for the 92, the 52 and the 85.6 per cent, and say which pairs can be compared.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 appear to contradict each other, yet on a like-for-like reading the field study did better. What explanations fit both?

Prototype testing

What watching eight people struggle with an unfinished thing can settle, and the much longer list of things it cannot.

1. Two desks, three months apart

On Tuesday 4 November 2025 Devyani Jhalani had nine working days before Vritti Work Cloud's January release train closed. Vritti sells payroll and approvals software to Indian mid-market employers: 410 customers, ₹86 crore of annual recurring revenue, filings that must survive EPFO, GSTN and the TDS schedules. The redesign on her desk concerned one thing: how a plant manager in Aurangabad delegates approval authority during two weeks of leave. That flow had generated 1,140 support tickets in the twelve months to September 2025. Twelve people had used the rebuilt version as a clickable prototype between 8 and 19 September. Her question was what twelve sessions entitled her to assert.

Three months later, on Monday 9 February 2026, Dhiren Jategaonkar faced a harder edge. Vimarsh Health Devices, Hyderabad, had ₹190 crore of Series B money and a camera-and-strip haemoglobin reader for home use, a CDSCO Class B device. In January eight people used a working-but-ugly build, four of them in their own homes; seven of the eight completed a reading unaided. But the app misread the strip 3 times in the 20 captures clean enough to score, and summative validation was booked for April. Locking the design meant validating a product that failed roughly one capture in seven; not locking it meant missing the pre-monsoon retail window.

Both turn on a question the field has argued for forty years: what does an incomplete artefact, put before a few real people, establish?

2. The idea, and the four camps

A prototype test is a procedure in which a representative user attempts a realistic task on a deliberately incomplete artefact while the team observes behaviour rather than opinion, to reduce one named risk before the cost of building properly is incurred. Four words carry it. Representative: from the population the decision depends on. Task: a goal the user already has, stated as a situation. Deliberately incomplete: the omissions are chosen, so the test isolates the risk. One named risk: of Cagan's four, value, usability, feasibility and viability, this instrument is strong on the second, partial on the first, silent on the rest.

Two roots met in the 1980s. The first is human factors: Alphonse Chapanis, examining B-17 landing accidents in 1943, found the flap and gear levers adjacent and identical, and recast pilot error as design error discoverable by watching. The second is cognitive psychology: Ericsson and Simon's Protocol Analysis (1980, 1984) made think-aloud defensible by specifying when verbalising corrupts the task. Gould and Lewis welded the two into practice in 1985: early focus on users, empirical measurement, iterative design. Kelley's 1983 Oz paradigm added the human behind the curtain; Houde and Hill (1997) classified prototypes by question rather than material; Buxton (2007) held that the sketch proposes and the prototype disposes.

Four camps disagree substantively. The measurement school (Nielsen; Sauro and Lewis) signs “five users per segment per iteration, iterated, finds most usability problems that matter” and refuses “five users can establish a success rate.” The generative school (Schrage, Buxton, the Stanford and Berkeley studios) signs “the artefact's job is to change the team's mind cheaply” and refuses “a prototype test yields a verdict.” The evidence-ladder school (Blank, Ries, Cagan, Torres) signs “a prototype test cannot price or forecast demand” and refuses “sessions are grounds to launch.” The regulated human-factors school (IEC 62366-1, the FDA's guidance) signs “formative and summative testing are different instruments” and refuses the heuristic for critical tasks.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice begins before recruitment, with a sentence of the form: we believe X; if it is false we do Y instead; this session shows it false by Z. Devyani's was that a plant manager finds delegation unprompted, failing which the entry point moves into the leave flow, shown false if a participant handed a leave request never reaches that screen. Without it, the debrief becomes an argument about which clip was memorable.

The quantitative treatment the field possesses is Nielsen and Landauer's 1993 model. Give each distinct problem a detection probability p, the chance one participant exposes it; the chance it is seen at least once in n independent sessions is 1 − (1 − p)n. The five-user argument is this expression at p = 0.31. The honest way to use it is to estimate p from your own matrix. Vritti's twelve sessions produced a grid of 20 problems against 12 participants, 240 cells, of which 69 recorded that participant hitting that problem.

Exhibit 1 — Vritti Work Cloud, delegation prototype, 12 sessions, 8–19 September 2025. Detection rate is detections divided by cells. For each class the last column is 1 − (1 − p)⁵; the total row's last cell is the problem-weighted average of the two cells above it, not that formula applied to the average p.
Problem classDistinct problemsCells (problems × 12)DetectionsDetection rate pSeen in 5 sessions

Every figure derives from the two counts in its own row. For blockers, 31 of the 48 cells were hits, or 64.6 per cent, so a blocker escapes five sessions with probability 0.354⁵ = 0.0056 and is seen with probability 99.4 per cent. For minor problems, 38 of 192 is 19.8 per cent, giving 66.8 per cent. The last row is not a sum: 69 of 240 cells is 28.8 per cent, and since four of the twenty problems block, 0.2 × 0.646 + 0.8 × 0.198 reproduces 0.288 exactly. The final column's total is also a weighted average, 0.2 × 99.4 + 0.8 × 66.8 = 73.3 per cent. It is emphatically not 1 − (1 − 0.288)⁵ = 81.6 per cent: the curve is non-linear in p, so feeding it an average detection rate overstates five-session coverage by eight points. Five sessions are near-certain to expose a task-stopping defect, while a third of the minor problems stay unseen, and that is where support volume lives.

Second-order mechanics are where competence shows. Fidelity is chosen against the risk, not the calendar: an artefact more finished than the question requires buys politeness, because participants stop criticising what looks shipped. Recruiting is behavioural, not demographic; Devyani's screener asked for managers who had filed a leave request within 60 days, disqualifying 23 of the 41 people her panel offered. The kill criterion is written first and analysis happens inside 24 hours.

The model is most often abused in benchmarking. Between 13 and 17 October, Vritti ran 10 fresh participants on the old flow and 10 on the new, same screener, same task: a two-step delegation unaided. Six of the ten succeeded on the old flow, nine of the ten on the new. The temptation is to report a 30-point improvement.

What 10 per arm can and cannot measure. For two proportions at 80 per cent power and a two-sided 5 per cent test, n per arm = (zα/2 + zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] ÷ (p₂−p₁)². With z = 1.96 and 0.84, (2.80)² = 7.84; p₁ = 0.60 gives 0.24 and p₂ = 0.90 gives 0.09, summing to 0.33; the difference 0.30 squared is 0.09. So 7.84 × 0.33 ÷ 0.09 = 28.75, or 29 per arm.

Backwards, at the sample she had: with a pooled rate of (6 + 9) ÷ 20 = 0.75, the minimum detectable effect at 10 per arm is 2.80 × √(2 × 0.75 × 0.25 ÷ 10) = 2.80 × 0.1936 = 54.2 percentage points. The observed 30-point gap sits inside it. Both use the normal approximation, crude at ten.

Devyani's analyst drew a narrower conclusion. The comparison does not license “better by 30 points”; a Fisher exact test on 6 of 10 against 9 of 10 returns p = 0.303. What licenses the build is mechanism, and the mechanism is specific. All four who failed on the old flow failed at the same step, searching a settings menu for delegation, and five of the six who succeeded there reached it only after opening that same menu. The new flow has no settings menu on that path; its single failure abandoned at the leave-date picker, a different step. The claim the sessions support is about the artefact, that the step which stopped four people is gone, not about rates ten per arm cannot resolve.

4. The conditions, as testable claims

Four conditions decide the instrument. One: the risk is comprehension or execution, not desire. Vritti passes; nobody doubts managers want to delegate during leave, only whether they can. Vimarsh passes on the interaction and fails on reading accuracy, a feasibility risk in usability clothing. Two: the behaviour can be elicited in minutes without the user's real stakes. Vritti passes; Vimarsh partly fails, since a 6 a.m. routine in a Hyderabad flat is not reproducible in a lab, so four of the eight sessions moved into homes. Three: the artefact can be made incomplete in the right places. Vimarsh fails hardest; you cannot fake optics. Four: the decision turns on the answer. If engineering is committed the test is theatre.

It is actively misleading in three situations. Where the question is willingness to pay it produces warm, useless data: participants are guests, and guests are polite. Where value accrues over weeks, a 50-minute session samples the wrong interval. Where the population that matters is adversarial rather than average, you want the hostile tail.

5. Hard edges

In two-sided markets the unit of test is the transaction, not the screen. Valaya Farm Network, a produce marketplace, learned this when buyer-side prototypes tested cleanly for four rounds while the mandi agents who set the listing were never in the room. The expert pattern is to prototype the handshake: one buyer, one agent, same hour, the facilitator watching the gap between what one side wrote and the other understood.

Regulated hardware replaces the heuristic with a rule. Under IEC 62366-1 Vimarsh's January sessions are formative: cheap, iterative, no prescribed size. April's exercise is summative validation, where the convention his notified body and US filing expect is fifteen participants per distinct user group. Vimarsh has three groups, self-testing adults over 55, family caregivers and community health workers, so 3 × 15 = 45 participants. Five and forty-five are not in conflict: one instrument discovers, the other conforms. Running 5 and calling it validation is a finding at audit.

AI-native products break the model's independence assumption. Vimarsh's reader misread 3 captures in 20, a point estimate of 15 per cent. Divija Jambhekar, his staff data scientist, put the Wilson 95 per cent interval on the page: with p̂ = 0.15, n = 20 and z = 1.96, the centre is (0.15 + 3.8416÷40) ÷ (1 + 3.8416÷20) = 0.24604 ÷ 1.19208 = 0.2064, and the half-width is (1.96÷1.19208) × √(0.006375 + 0.002401) = 1.6442 × 0.09368 = 0.1541. The interval runs from 5.2 to 36.0 per cent. One of those is a shippable device; the other is a recall.

At the organisational seams two leaks recur. The first is the prototype that escapes into a sales demo: a clickable flow shown to a procurement committee becomes a de facto commitment, and Vritti's rule that prototypes never leave research custody exists because a 2024 renewal was negotiated against a screen that did not exist. The second is the prototype that becomes the specification, being the only artefact anyone can see. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than their talks suggest: usually one researcher has the standing to say “that is not what we tested”.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The expert tests the riskiest assumption, not the newest screen. The tell is the session plan: a competent one walks the flow in order, an expert one spends 30 of 50 minutes on a single step. The obvious reading, cover everything while you have the user, is wrong: coverage buys shallow evidence on ten questions when one decides.

The expert distrusts a clean test. Dharini Jariwala, Vritti's principal researcher, treats a round in which nothing broke as a recruiting failure; the tell is the screener, since clean rounds usually mean participants too expert or forewarned. The obvious reading is that the design is good; the likelier one is that the task was too easy to fail.

The expert separates the observed from the inferred, out loud. The tell is debrief vocabulary: “four of twelve never found it” against “users can't find it.” The second sentence contains a population; the session has none. Dharini calls this the commonest route by which a well-run study yields a wrong decision.

The expert chooses fidelity downward under time pressure. Under deadline the instinct is to test whatever is nearly built. The tell is polish relative to the question's age: a new question inside a pixel-perfect screen gets no honest answer, because participants calibrate criticism to apparent investment.

The expert builds the task from the user's situation, not the product's structure. “Your plant head is on leave from Monday; sort out approvals” produces different behaviour from “delegate approval authority.” The tell is whether the product's nouns appear in the task text; if they do, the test reports the team's vocabulary back as the user's.

The expert treats stated intention as weak and directional, and tracks the same individuals forward. In March 2025 Vritti tested a weekly approval digest with 14 participants; 11 were in accounts that joined the April pilot, and 9 of those 11 said they would open it every week. In the first four weeks, 3 of those 9 did, which is 33 per cent on a 95 per cent interval of 12 to 65 per cent. The tell is whether anyone can name the individuals in both columns: comparing those 9 in 11 against an adoption rate over every pilot account is the error, and nine people cannot estimate a rate at all.

The expert knows when the prototype is the wrong rung. The tell is the question's verb: “can they?” is a prototype question, “will they pay?” belongs to pre-sales, deposits or a painted door. An expert cancels a booked round and spends the money on a landing page instead.

Finally, the expert prices late discovery to defend the budget. Vritti logs where each usability defect in approvals was caught and what it cost.

Exhibit 2 — Vritti Work Cloud, 38 usability defects in the approvals area, 24 months to 30 September 2025. Engineer-day figures are medians, so the last row is a weighted average and not a sum.

Medians do not add, so the page does not claim 287.5 engineer-days were spent. Devyani's budget case is a counterfactual at median rates: moving the three post-release defects to pilot is 3 × (41 − 14) = 81 median-days, or ₹14.58 lakh at ₹18,000 fully loaded. She flags both weaknesses: the ledger records where defects were found, not where they could have been, and a skewed distribution makes a median a poor proxy for a cost. Boehm's 1:10:100 curve has been disputed for twenty years on that point.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is recruitment honesty: participants from your own community flatter you, and sessions are cheap enough that teams run too many and too few commitment tests. In B2B and enterprise the user and the buyer differ, so a test that delights eight end users says nothing about a procurement committee. In marketplaces the object of study is the handshake between sides. In hardware the axes come apart: a looks-like model answers grip, a works-like rig answers timing, and they cannot merge until tooling is committed. In AI products behaviour is the product, so Wizard of Oz is powerful early and dangerous late, the confederate being better than the model.

By stage the difference is smaller than the literature suggests: seed teams and listed companies both learn most from the first five sessions. What changes is the cost of being wrong, and so the standard of proof. The seed team can act on four sessions because its reversal cost is a fortnight, while Vritti's is a release train and 410 renewal conversations. At scale, research's second function, convincing people who were not in the room, dominates the first.

8. Three worked examples

Vritti, delegation flow, worked above: twelve sessions, 20 problems of which 4 blocking, a 10-versus-10 comparison against a 54.2-point minimum detectable effect, and a build justified on mechanism rather than rate.

Vimarsh, strip reader: eight formative sessions, seven completions, 3 misreads in 20 scored captures, interval 5.2 to 36.0 per cent. The test did its job; the answer concerned feasibility, not usability. Dhiren's instrument for the rate is a bench harness of 240 captures across lighting conditions, narrowing the interval to about 9 points.

Vagmi Learning, where it failed. In November 2025 the Bengaluru study-skills app tested a paid tier in ten sessions. Nine of the ten completed the subscribe-and-set-a-goal task; eight of the ten said they would pay ₹299 a month. Participants came from Vagmi's own free-user community, thanked with ₹800 vouchers. Damini Jagdale's team read this as demand and launched on 2 March 2026. By 30 April, of the 4,210 visitors who reached the pricing page, 61 started checkout and 23 paid; that is 0.55 per cent of 4,210. Of the 61 who began, 23 finished, or 37.7 per cent. The test measured whether people could subscribe, and they could; the failure was the inference.

Recovery meant changing instrument. Between 19 May and 2 June 2026 Vagmi ran a painted door asking for a ₹99 refundable deposit.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Four failure modes do most of the damage, each with an early sign.

The pattern is the same in all four: a competent test, then a question it was not built to answer. Hence diagnostics about provenance, not method.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is not whether to prototype but what the test is for. The measurement position holds that usability is a quantity and small-sample discovery is well understood; its evidence is three decades of replications of the discovery curve. It would be wrong if detection probabilities were more heterogeneous than the model assumes, and Exhibit 1 shows they are: 0.646 and 0.198 are not one parameter.

The generative position holds that the measurement framing kills the instrument's value: the artefact exists to provoke a better idea, and scoring it turns a design conversation into an audit. Its evidence is the studio record, the products whose shape changed after a session that scored as a pass. It would be wrong if teams converged on good designs unmeasured, which they do not.

The live-traffic position holds both are pre-industrial: one per cent of real traffic behind a flag measures behaviour with real stakes at a sample size that supports inference. It is wrong where there is no traffic to split, the change is too large to flag, regulation requires validation first, or the mechanism matters more than the rate; Vimarsh cannot A/B test a recall. Nobody has reconciled them.

11. What mastery looks like

Four habits are visible. The master spends longer on the sentence stating the assumption than on the prototype. She can say which of her last five decisions a prototype test changed; if none, that is a finding about her process. She drops fidelity as pressure rises. And she tells a steering meeting when a study cannot answer the question asked.

12. Two decisions, and questions for discussion

Devyani committed the six weeks of build on 7 November 2025, on narrower grounds than her deck first claimed: not that the new flow was 30 points better, since at p = 0.303 that contrast is worth nothing, but that the step her support lead had coded as the largest source of those 1,140 tickets was seen stopping four people and is absent from the new flow by inspection. She also funded a third round of five sessions against the minor tail, where the class curve puts coverage at 92.9 per cent after twelve sessions, counting only problems those twelve could see.

Dhiren did not lock the design. He split the question: the interaction was settled enough to freeze, and the misread rate was never a usability question, so the 240-capture harness went in ahead of April's validation. Vimarsh missed the pre-monsoon window by five weeks.

1. Devyani's benchmark could not distinguish a 30-point improvement from noise. Was the build unjustified, or is mechanism a legitimate substitute for a rate?

2. Vagmi's ten sessions were well run. Where should the error have been caught: design, readout, or launch? Who owned it?

3. Vimarsh's five-user and forty-five-participant protocols coexist. For which of your products would a summative standard change what you ship, and at what cost?

13. Going deeper

  1. Designing discovery experiments: picks which assumption earns a test.
  2. Wireframes, mockups, prototypes: incomplete in the right places.
  3. Design sprints: the packaged five-day form.
  4. The four product risks: this instrument's boundary.
  5. Landing-page and smoke tests: the rung for “will they”.
  6. Fake doors and painted doors: cold demand, usable sample size.
  7. Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests: behaviour you cannot yet build.
  8. Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits: evidence with money attached.
  9. The evidence ladder: which rung you are on, and the next one's price.

Prototype Testing: Watching Someone Try to Use What You Have Only Drawn

A case-style explainer for the reader who must run, and judge, a prototype test next week.

1. The Monday brief

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Pranita Vanjari, a senior product manager at Jhankar Pay, opened the planning document that would decide her quarter. Jhankar Pay is a Pune-based payments app that small shopkeepers use to accept UPI (Unified Payments Interface, the interbank instant-payment system run by NPCI, the National Payments Corporation of India) and to run a simple daily sales book. Jhankar Pay's retention data showed that merchants who recorded credit sales stayed far longer than those who only took payments.

The proposal was an automated udhaar feature. Udhaar, the Hindi word for credit given to a customer, is the ledger most kirana (neighbourhood grocery) owners still keep on paper. The feature would let a shopkeeper log what a customer owed and send a polite WhatsApp or SMS reminder in a tone of the shopkeeper's choosing. Pramod Varghese, the head of engineering, had quoted 14 weeks for six engineers: 84 engineer-weeks, which at a loaded cost of ₹60,000 per engineer-week is ₹50.4 lakh. If the feature failed to change behaviour, the quarter and the money would be gone.

Pranita doubted the screens, not the idea. Her designer, Prisha Valanju, had built a clickable prototype in a week, and Pranita proposed a round of sessions with eight shopkeepers before committing the engineers. Varghese objected: eight people was not a sample. Both were partly right.

2. The idea

A prototype is a simulation of a product detailed enough to be used for a task but not built to run. A prototype test puts that simulation in front of people from the intended audience, asks them to attempt realistic tasks, and records what they do. The task must resemble the participant's own goal, and the evidence is behaviour, not opinion.

The method descends from usability engineering in the 1980s, when software firms found that expensive code was being written for screens ordinary users could not operate. Jakob Nielsen and Thomas Landauer published a widely cited 1993 model of how many problems small samples reveal (Nielsen and Landauer, 1993). Design consultancies later extended it from usability to desirability.

The problem it solves is the cost asymmetry of discovery. A flaw found in a drawing costs an afternoon; found after release, it costs an engineering cycle plus the users lost. The sentence Pranita could repeat without sounding glib: "We are not asking whether people like it; we are watching whether they can do it, and whether they will give us something real for it."

Figure 2 locates the technique. Value risk is whether anyone wants the outcome; usability risk is whether they can get it; feasibility risk is whether the team can build it; viability risk is whether the business works. A prototype reveals the first two, because both show in behaviour in front of a screen. The other two need engineers and finance.

3. How it actually works

The first step is the one most often skipped: naming the risk and writing the pass bar, the result that would justify proceeding, before any session. Pranita wrote two bars. Usability: at least 6 of 8 shopkeepers send a scripted reminder unaided. Value: a behavioural commitment, not a compliment, which she defined as the shopkeeper photographing one page of their own paper ledger so Jhankar Pay could pre-load it.

Recruitment (step 2) meant eight current Jhankar Pay merchants who already gave credit, not colleagues. Each received ₹1,500 for forty minutes. Task scripting (step 3) stated a goal in the shopkeeper's words: "Suman-ji owes you ₹1,850 from last week. Get her a reminder that is polite." It never named a button.

Observation (step 4) has implicit rules. The facilitator stays silent while the participant struggles, because rescuing them destroys the data; asked "what should I press?", she answers "what would you press if I were not here?". A second person logs events. Logging (step 5) is where the discipline lies: each row records an observation (what happened), kept apart from an interpretation (why the team thinks it happened). Teams that merge the two end up with opinions. Step 6 compares counts with the bars written in step 1.

4. A worked example, line by line

Round 1 ran on Wednesday 7 and Thursday 8 October with eight shopkeepers. Table 1 shows every usability problem observed and how many of the eight encountered it.

Table 1. Round 1 problems, base = 8 merchants

A. Tone selector hidden in an overflow menu562.5%

Problem A affected 5 of 8, which is 62.5 per cent. The average row divides the 11 encounters by 32, which is 4 problems times 8 merchants, giving 34.4 per cent. Of the 5 who met problem A, 2 eventually found the selector and 3 gave up. So the unaided completion count was 8 minus 3, or 5 of 8. That missed the bar of 6 by one person, and every failure traced to the same hidden menu.

The value measure was separate. Seven of eight said they would use the feature daily (87.5 per cent). But only 3 of 8 photographed a ledger page (37.5 per cent). Pranita weighted the behaviour, not the sentence.

Now the sample-size question Varghese raised. If a problem affects a share p of users, the chance that n sessions see it at least once is 1 − (1 − p)n, because (1 − p)n is the chance that every one of the n misses it. For a problem hitting one merchant in four (p = 0.25), five sessions give 1 − 0.755 = 1 − 0.2373 = 76.3 per cent, and eight give 1 − 0.758 = 1 − 0.1001 = 90.0 per cent.

Second pass: change one input. Hold the eight sessions and lower p to 0.10, a problem that bites one merchant in ten. Eight sessions now give 1 − 0.98 = 1 − 0.4305 = 57.0 per cent, the amber bar at the right of Figure 4. Reaching 85 per cent for this rarer problem would need 19 sessions (18 give 84.99 per cent), against 7 for the common one. A small test reliably detects frequent problems and poorly detects rare ones.

The team then fixed A (tone selector moved onto the main screen) and B (due date blank and required), and ran Round 2 on Friday 9 October with eight new merchants. Seven of 8 completed unaided; problems A and B appeared 0 times; C appeared twice; a new problem, E (the amount keypad lacked lakh separators), appeared once; and 4 of 8 photographed a ledger page. Had problem A still affected 62.5 per cent of users, the chance of seeing it in none of eight sessions is 0.3758, about 0.04 per cent; this takes the observed rate as the true one. Even at Round 1's interval floor of 30.6 per cent, the chance is 0.6948, about 5.4 per cent, so the fix is probably real. The completion rise from 5 of 8 to 7 of 8 is a different matter (section 5).

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Observation is not opinion

The same eight people produced both figures. What they said and what they did came apart by 50 percentage points (87.5 minus 37.5).

Small samples find problems; they do not measure rates

A Wilson interval (a standard bound on a proportion from a small count) turns 7 of 8 into a range of 52.9 to 97.8 per cent, as in Table 2. Round 1's 5 of 8 gives 30.6 to 86.3 per cent. The ranges overlap by about half (52.9 to 86.3 per cent), so the test cannot say the completion rate rose. It can say that a specific, observed obstacle vanished. Those are different claims, and only the second is supported.

Fidelity should match the question

Fidelity is how closely the prototype resembles the finished product. Paper suits layout questions, clickable screens suit task flows. Choose the lowest level that still lets the participant attempt the real task.

Participants are not the market

Eight current Jhankar Pay merchants are a recruited convenience sample. Being comfortable with the app, they will find the feature easier than a lapsed user would.

Confusion with its neighbours

A prototype test is not a survey or an A/B test. A survey asks what people say; an A/B test measures what thousands do with released code; a prototype test observes what a few do with unreleased screens.

The facilitator is part of the instrument

Leading questions ("Did you find the tone menu easy?") and kindly hints change the result; scripts and silence rules are the calibration.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether merchants will still use the feature in month three, whether reminder wording will sour a customer relationship, or whether messaging costs leave a margin. Before relying on any result, ask: who was recruited, what was the bar before the test, what was the base, and which claim would a different sample overturn?

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

Table 3. Prototype testing in context
SettingWhat changes
ConsumerRecruitment is cheap; participants are polite strangers, so behavioural asks (a pre-order, a shared contact) matter.
B2BThe user is not always the buyer: a clerk can finish the task while the finance head blocks the purchase. Test both roles.
MarketplaceTwo sides must be tested, and a prototype cannot simulate liquidity.
Early-stage companyNo research function: the founder facilitates, risking leading questions. Paper prototypes dominate.
Large companyPanels and research teams make rounds repeatable but slow; the risk is a ritual test that approves whatever is shown.

Jhankar Pay sits between: a designer and a recruiting budget but no lab, so Pranita could run a round in two days but had to guard against her own team's wish for good news. The same technique protects different assumptions in each setting, so the pass bar must change accordingly.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Four failures, how they show, and the cheapest check
MistakeSymptom from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Testing opinionsReport full of quotes such as "loved it"Believing stated intent predicts actionAsk: what did participants give up or do?
No pre-set barEvery result is read as encouragingTreating the test as discovery, not decisionFind the bar's date; if it follows the sessions, there is no bar
Rescuing participants100% completion in a confusing flowSeeing silence as rudenessCount facilitator interventions per session
Over-reading rates"Completion rose from 62.5% to 87.5%" from 8 vs 8Forgetting small-sample interval widthWrite the interval next to the headline figure

None of these needs more participants; each needs earlier writing of the bar, the script and the intervention count.

8. What good looks like

The target is Pranita's second round: a stated risk, a bar written before the sessions, eight users from the intended group, a silent facilitator, a log that separates seeing from guessing, and a report that separates what was observed (obstacles vanished) from what stayed unknown (completion rate). In cost terms, the two rounds cost ₹1.8 lakh and ₹1.1 lakh, ₹2.9 lakh in all, which is 5.8 per cent of the ₹50.4 lakh build they informed.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Monday 12 October Pranita did not ask for the 14-week build. Round 2 cleared the usability bar (7 of 8 against 6) but the value signal was soft: 4 of 8 handing over a ledger page is encouraging and cannot be told apart from 3 of 8. She asked instead for a thin slice, reminders plus ledger import, at 6 engineers for 6 weeks: 36 engineer-weeks, ₹21.6 lakh, 42.9 per cent of the original quote. The slice would go to 40 pilot merchants with a bar stated in advance: at least half importing their ledger within 14 days. Varghese accepted, provided the pilot, not the prototype, decided the remainder.

Her reasoning is the thread of this page. The test earned the right to spend ₹21.6 lakh by removing a documented obstacle and giving a modest behavioural signal. It did not earn ₹50.4 lakh, because it could not measure retention, economics or rare problems. Next, learn design sprints, the five-day format in which a team builds and tests a prototype in one week; they compress this loop into a routine and show where it needs discipline.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the ledger-photo rate had been 3 of 8 in both rounds, what would you have wanted the pilot to measure, and what bar would you set? Second, think of a decision in your own work where people say they would use something: what is the cheapest costly behaviour you could ask them for instead?

Rutuvan Foods: Two Hundred Deposits

A decision case on landing-page and smoke tests

1. Opening

At 8:40 on the morning of Thursday 15 October 2026, Chaitali Jathar sat in the Rutuvan Foods office in Pune with a dashboard open and a deadline eight days away. The company's two-week landing-page test for a new subscription product had closed the previous night. Two hundred people had each paid a refundable ₹199 deposit to reserve a place. The test's own pass mark, written down on 28 September, had been 160.

By Friday 23 October, Chaitali, the head of product, had to tell Charuhas Jamdade, the founder and chief executive, whether Rutuvan should sign a contract kitchen in Chakan. Signing would commit ₹42 lakh at once and open production capacity from Monday 2 November. Charuhas had said that two hundred was an answer. Chaitali was not yet sure which question it answered.

2. Company background

Rutuvan Foods was founded in Pune in 2019 and sells millet snacks: ragi chips, jowar puffs and a foxtail-millet granola. Revenue for FY2026 (April 2025 to March 2026) was ₹38 crore. The products sell through the company's own site, Amazon, BigBasket, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, and 41,000 customers have given an email address. Tata Soulfull and Slurrp Farm sell millet foods at national scale, and Yoga Bar competes for the same shelf.

The new product, provisionally called Rutu Box, would cost ₹1,499 a month. It would deliver sixteen heat-and-eat millet meals every fortnight, drawn from Maharashtrian, Konkani and Karnataka kitchens. Billing would run through Razorpay, with UPI AutoPay mandates under NPCI rules and the RBI's recurring-payment framework. Unlike the snacks, the box needs dedicated cooking capacity, new pouch tooling and a subscription system, so Charuhas wanted evidence before spending.

3. The situation

The hypothesis, set down on 28 September, was that at least 1.0 per cent of visitors to a single landing page would pay the ₹199 deposit within fourteen days. The planned 16,000 visitors made the pass mark 160 deposits. The page ran from 1 to 14 October. It carried the price, a sample menu and a DPDP Act consent notice, and asked first for an email and phone number, then for a UPI deposit. A sign-up costs nothing; a deposit costs money, so the team treated deposits as the signal. Exhibit 1 sets out the result by traffic source.

Headline first: 200 deposits from 16,000 visitors is 1.25 per cent, a quarter above the bar. Chaitali then split the table by who had been asked. The email and WhatsApp traffic, 4,000 visitors who already knew Rutuvan, produced 132 deposits, or 3.30 per cent. The 12,000 cold visitors from Meta and Google produced 68, or 0.57 per cent. Two-thirds of the deposits, 66 per cent, came from people who knew the brand.

The team saw this from three cities. In Berlin, the designer Chinar Jawale, who had built the page in six days, noted that the Meta visitors scrolled to the price and left. In Toronto, the data scientist Charmi Jangam sent a note at 6:00 pm Pune time on Wednesday, 8:30 am for her, warning that the pooled rate hid a mix effect and that the test had run in the weeks before Diwali (Sunday 8 November), when food-gifting interest is unusually high. In New Jersey, the sales head Chiranjit Jambhale, nine and a half hours behind Pune until the clocks change on 1 November, reported that non-resident customers kept asking whether the box could be sent to parents in India.

4. The people

Charuhas Jamdade, founder and chief executive, Pune, wants to sign. He reads 1.25 per cent as a pass, and distrusts a second test that would push the launch past the festival season.

Charmi Jangam, data scientist, Toronto, wants the result judged on the audience the business will have to buy. The list of 41,000 has been mailed once, so the warm audience is largely spent.

Chinar Jawale, designer, Berlin, wants a fair chance to fix the page. He thinks the price appeared before the value was explained and that a better sequence would lift cold conversion.

Chiranjit Jambhale, sales head, New Jersey, wants a gift version for the diaspora. He values speed and has no data on how many would pay.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 shows the launch cost, Exhibit 3 plots the Exhibit 1 rates against the bar, and Figure 1 lays out the calendar.

6. The options

Option A: sign by 23 October and launch. Rutuvan commits the ₹42 lakh in Exhibit 2, starts cooking on 2 November and spends the remaining ₹20 lakh after launch. The upside is speed and the warm demand already in hand. The cost is that ₹42 lakh is gone whatever happens next. If the ₹62 lakh is to be recovered within the first twelve months, break-even needs an average of about 1,033 active subscribers (12,400 box-months divided by 12). Even if every one of the 200 depositors subscribed and stayed a full year, that would be 2,400 box-months, about 19 per cent of the requirement. At the cold cost of ₹2,647 per deposit, the ₹11 lakh marketing line buys roughly 416 more deposits, not subscribers.

Option B: do not sign; run a cold-traffic retest. Rutuvan keeps the same page logic and the same ₹199 deposit, so results stay comparable, but buys only Google search traffic, the one cold source that met the bar. At the test's ₹25 per visitor, if that holds at five times the volume, ₹3 lakh buys 12,000 visitors after Diwali, from Monday 16 November to Sunday 29 November. The kitchen's next slot, from 11 January 2027, stays open until 14 December. The cost is ten weeks of delay and a missed festival season.

Option C: shelve the box. Rutuvan refunds the ₹39,800 of deposits and puts the effort into snack pack sizes on Zepto and Swiggy Instamart. The cost is abandoning the one concept that earned 3.30 per cent from the people who know the brand best.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the test measure, and why did the team treat a ₹199 deposit as stronger evidence than 2,416 sign-ups?
  2. Was 1.0 per cent of all visitors the right bar, and the right base? Recompute the result for the audience Rutuvan will have to win after launch.
  3. What must be true of subscriber numbers for ₹62 lakh to be recovered, and how much does Exhibit 1 say about that?
  4. Which option would you take on 23 October, and what result in the next test would change your mind before you commit the money?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A smoke test asks whether anyone will show intent before the product exists. Three things make the answer trustworthy: an action that costs the visitor something, an audience that resembles the one the business must win, and a pass mark fixed in advance. Rutuvan did the first and third well; the second failed quietly, because the pooled 1.25 per cent mixed a spent warm audience with a cold one.

One defensible path: Option B. Cold traffic converted at 0.57 per cent, below the bar, and 132 warm depositors cannot supply the 1,033 average subscribers the launch needs. Option A risks ₹42 lakh on the strength of people Rutuvan can reach only once. Option B risks ₹3 lakh, about 7 per cent of the amount committed on signing (3 over 42), to learn what only a larger cold sample can show. Google's 30 deposits are too few to say whether 1.25 per cent is real. Set the rule before the test: 120 or more deposits from 12,000 visitors (1.0 per cent) means sign for January; 60 or fewer (0.5 per cent) means shelve; anything between means revise the offer and test again. Option C is premature while the search result is still open.

Limits. A pass still does not show retention or delivery quality, and at Google's observed ₹2,000 a deposit the ₹11 lakh marketing line buys 550 deposits, 750 with the 200 in hand, still short of 1,033 even if every deposit became a year-long subscriber. A pass earns the right to a smaller, staged commitment, the step MVP types addresses. Option A with a smaller kitchen commitment negotiated first is also defensible; launching on the headline 1.25 per cent is not.

Landing-page and smoke tests

Measuring intent before the product exists — and the four denominators that decide what it means.

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On 19 March 2026 Giridhar Kanitkar had one slide on the wall and ninety minutes to decide what it meant. Kanitkar ran growth at Yuvasetu Learning in Bengaluru, whose exam-preparation app had about 1.9 lakh monthly active users. For fourteen days, from 2 to 15 March, Yuvasetu had bought traffic to a page for a product that did not exist: Interview Coach, a ₹499-a-month service to rehearse campus-placement interviews and score the answers. The page served 412,000 impressions, drew 8,240 clicks and collected 361 email addresses; 148 of those people reached a refundable ₹49 reservation and 37 paid. The slide said 5.07 per cent; the build was costed at ₹2.4 crore. Kanitkar had four numbers he could honestly have put on that slide, and his choice would decide the question.

Five weeks later Geetanjali Kelshikar faced the mirror image. Kelshikar was chief product officer at Yantrashala Systems, a Pune firm making battery-powered cold-chain loggers and the dashboard that read them, sold to pharmacy chains, dairy unions and vaccine logistics firms. A third-generation logger needed ₹2.1 crore of tooling and firmware before a unit could ship. At the 24 April board meeting a director asked why, before spending that, Yantrashala should not spend ₹9.6 lakh on a landing page and advertising.

Kelshikar's answer — that in her market a landing page could not produce a number worth reading — sounded like an excuse, and she had eight weeks to show otherwise. The two cases are this topic's poles.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A smoke test offers a product that does not yet exist and measures how many people take a costly action in response. A landing-page test is its commonest form: one page describing the offer, traffic driven to it deliberately, one measured act — a click, an email address, a deposit. The name, borrowed from electronics bench practice, carries the right connotation: a cheap test licensed to say stop with confidence and never to say go.

The history runs through direct-response advertising long before software. Split-run mail testing with keyed coupons had by the 1920s established the finding that still governs the practice: a coupon's absolute response rate transferred almost not at all, moving with list, season and postage, while the ordering between two coupons mailed into one list on one day was stable. The modern vocabulary arrived with the lean-startup literature after 2008 and Alberto Savoia's "pretotyping"; Buffer's pricing page behind a signup button and Dropbox's waiting-list video became folklore.

Four positions contend, and no synthesis reconciles them. Demand-first signs that a difference in signup rate between two propositions, on the same traffic in one window, is decision-grade evidence about which to build; it will not sign that the absolute signup rate predicts the absolute purchase rate. Commitment signs that only a rate measured on an act costing the prospect money or reputation may be projected forward; it will not sign that a free email capture is therefore worthless. Research design — taught by the studio programmes, Berkeley's SCET, Stanford's design-methods sequence and Cornell Tech's product studio all requiring a material assumption tested on a real product and the design reported — signs that an underpowered test is worse than none. Feasibility-first signs that risks be tested in order of probability times cost, demand rarely being binding in hardware and AI-native work; it will not sign that demand tests are never worth running early. Kelshikar belongs here.

3. Mechanics: the denominator problem, worked

Kanitkar's slide holds the hazard in one cell: a single numerator, 361 email signups counted at 23:59 on 15 March 2026, and four defensible denominators.

Exhibit 1 — Yuvasetu Interview Coach: the measured funnel, 2–15 March 2026
StageCountWhat the count is
Impressions412,000Ad views, both platforms
Clicks8,240Billed at ₹33.00
Sessions7,540Page loads completed
Unique visitors7,120Distinct devices
Qualified visitors4,270Passed both screens
Email signups361Address submitted
Reached reservation page148Clicked through
Paid ₹49 reservation37Card charged, refundable

The screens above the form asked job-search status and years of experience.

Three rates follow, and then a ceiling. Against impressions, 361 of 412,000 is 0.0876 per cent. Against sessions, 361 of 7,540 is 4.79 per cent. Against unique visitors, 361 of 7,120 is 5.07 per cent — the slide. The fourth figure is not a rate: 361 of 4,270 is 8.45 per cent, but visitors who answered neither screen still saw the form, so the 361 is not confined to the 4,270. It is an upper bound on the qualified-visitor rate. Narrowest base to widest is a factor of ninety-six.

Hence the habit: never state a smoke-test rate without naming its base and counting date in the same sentence. The qualified-visitor ceiling is the most flattering of the four and the least usable: its numerator overflows its denominator, and the screen producing the 4,270 is answered voluntarily, selecting for engagement before the measured act.

Exhibit 3 — Cost of the Yuvasetu smoke test
ItemAmount (₹)
Paid media2,71,920
Page build and creative48,080
Total3,20,000

Media: 8,240 clicks at ₹33.00, or ₹660.00 per thousand impressions at the observed 2.00 per cent click-through. On the total: ₹886.43 per email signup, ₹8,648.65 per paid reservation.

The power calculation nobody runs

A smoke test is a two-proportion comparison, and its sample follows from the baseline rate, the difference worth detecting and the error rates accepted. In the pooled normal approximation, with p̄ the average of the two rates and δ their difference, at 5 per cent significance and 80 per cent power:

n per arm = 2 × p̄ × (1 − p̄) × (1.96 + 0.84)2 ÷ δ2

Take the signup rate: baseline 5.07 per cent on unique visitors; round to 5.0 and ask to detect a rival at 7.0. Then p̄ = 0.06, p̄(1 − p̄) = 0.0564 and (1.96 + 0.84)2 = 7.84, so n = 2 × 0.0564 × 7.84 ÷ 0.0202 = 0.884352 ÷ 0.0004 = 2,211 per arm, 4,422 for two — under nine days at the observed 7,120 over fourteen days, or 508.6 a day. Kanitkar, though, cared about the reservation rate: 37 against 7,120 unique visitors is 0.52 per cent. To detect a rise to 0.78 per cent, p̄ = 0.0065 and δ = 0.0026, so n = 2 × 0.0065 × 0.9935 × 7.84 ÷ 0.00262 = 0.10125752 ÷ 0.00000676 = 14,979 per arm, 29,958 in all — 6.8 times as much, and fifty-nine days.

The steps left implicit

Competent practitioners run the page. Experts do five things first and one afterwards. They write down the decision the test must change and the rate at which they would make each choice; fix the base and counting method in writing; choose the ask on the ladder below rather than defaulting to an email field; compute the sample it needs; and pin the traffic split, since a platform's optimiser will otherwise chase whichever creative converts and wreck the randomisation. Afterwards they telephone the converters: only the conversations say why.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Six claims, each true or false of a case. C1. The binding risk is demand, not feasibility. True for Yuvasetu; false for Yantrashala, where firmware and battery life were open and category demand was already evidenced by competitors. C2. The offer can be stated truthfully on one screen. True of Interview Coach; only partly, of a logger whose value turns on a certificate and an integration. C3. The traffic you can buy resembles the market you would serve. True for Yuvasetu, decisively false for Yantrashala. C4. The universe is large enough to power the comparison. True at 7,120 visitors a fortnight, false at Yantrashala's scale. C5. The ask can carry a real cost. True of the ₹49 reservation, and for Yantrashala too, but only through a conversation. C6. A false positive is recoverable. True at a ₹62 lakh build, much less so at ₹2.1 crore of unrepurposable tooling.

Exhibit 6 — Why a landing page cannot resolve Yantrashala's question
QuantityValueSource
Operators in the Indian universe1,840Sites with 25+ controlled points
Reachable by advertising994Named buyer on a trade list
Form-fills at a 3% rate30Category benchmark
Rate on reachable base3.02%30 ÷ 994
Standard error of the rate0.543 ptsBinomial, n = 994
95% interval, lower1.96%3.02 − 1.96 × 0.543
95% interval, upper4.08%3.02 + 1.96 × 0.543

The reachable base is 994 of 1,840 operators, or 54.0 per cent, from the April 2026 trade list. The interval spans a factor of just over two: the defect is resolution, not accuracy.

The idea is actively misleading, not merely weak, in four situations. Where stated intent and revealed behaviour diverge systematically — education, health, personal finance, sustainability — the page measures aspiration and charges a build to find out. Where demand depends on distribution you lack, a high rate on bought traffic forecasts nothing about organic reach. Where regulation governs what may be advertised, as with insurance and credit under IRDAI and RBI norms, the page cannot state the real terms, so measured intent attaches to an offer that will never exist. And where the product is a behaviour change, signing up is the easy part.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In a multi-product company a fake door inside an existing app measures switching, not new demand, and is contaminated by the installed base's trust in the brand; Kanitkar refused that route because his question was whether strangers would pay. In a two-sided market a one-sided test is close to uninformative, since demand-side conversion depends on supply liquidity that does not exist; the disciplined form is a paired test, both sides in one window, the demand rate read as a lower bound.

In regulated categories the compliance review is a free pre-mortem: if legal will not let the page say it, the product cannot promise it. In hardware plus software the commitment is lumpy and irreversible, so the only worthwhile test is a refundable deposit against a dated delivery; refundability is what keeps it a test. In AI-native products the page describes an output quality, and demand for a quality the system cannot reach is a real signal attached to the wrong product.

At the seams, four groups read one rate against four bases: growth quotes qualified visitors, finance needs impressions, product should want the reservation cell, legal reads the copy. Mature companies answer with infrastructure — a standing harness with a fixed template and base definition, so this quarter's 5.07 per cent is commensurable with last quarter's. They say they decide on the rate; they also weigh the converter debrief and whether a sponsor will stake a year on it.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The denominator is a choice, and whoever picks it picks the answer. The tell is a rate quoted without a base in the same sentence. It is no technicality: the base is the only thing making the rate comparable to anything, including the pre-set threshold.

A signup is intent; only money is purchase. The tell is "conversion" in a sentence containing no price. The obvious reading is that intent proxies purchase at a fixed discount. It is not: the discount widens with the promise's credibility, so the signal is worst where it looks best.

Traffic source is part of the treatment. The tell is a rate compared across two months with no channel-mix table beside it: a change of audience is a change of experiment.

The level barely transfers; the ordering between arms does. The tell is a threshold written as a bare percentage with no prior from a comparable page. This is split-run mail's hundred-year-old lesson, and why a single-arm test is weak.

The platform's optimiser is an unmeasured confound. The tell is unequal impressions across arms at the run's end. The platform looks to have found the winner; in fact it reallocated on early noise, so the arms differ in audience too.

The page becomes the specification. The tell is a sentence the roadmap cannot ship within two quarters. Teams read the page as marketing; the market reads a contract. Price, guarantee, delivery promise and bundle all sat inside the treatment, so changing any invalidates the rate.

The interesting cell is almost always the underpowered one. The tell is a decision resting on fewer than about forty events in it. A large top of funnel feels well powered, but power follows the rarest measured event.

The real output is a list of people, not a number. The tell is that nobody has telephoned a converter a week later. The rate decides whether to proceed; the conversations decide what to build.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the method is strongest: large universes, cheap traffic, a buyer who is user and payer too. In B2B it works where the buying unit is one or two people and the price sits on a card. In enterprise it fails C3 and C4 together; the substitute is account-based — named accounts, letters of intent, paid pilots. In platforms and marketplaces the difficulty is the pairing. For hardware, the deposit. For AI products the signal is easy to get and usually attached to a capability that does not yet exist.

Stage changes the threshold, not the method. A seed-stage team can act on a weak signal because its alternative is no information; a company carrying ₹2.1 crore of tooling needs one that survives a board. The other stage difference is the fake door's cost: a company with no brand has no trust to spend.

8. Three worked examples

Yuvasetu: the signal held, and the ordering was what held

Kanitkar built a ₹62 lakh thin version, shipped 11 June 2026. Of the 361 addresses, 309 were reachable at launch: 29 of the 37 reservation-payers, and 280 of the 324 who had given only an email. In the first month, to 10 July 2026, 46 subscribed at ₹499.

Gopinath Kattimani, the analyst, caught the error in the review's first draft, which set the reservation cohort's 21 of 29 (72.4 per cent) against the overall 46 of 309 (14.89 per cent) and called the gap fivefold. But the 309 contains the 29 and the 46 contains the 21, so the figures are not independent. The like-for-like pair is reservation-payers against email-only signups: 21 of 29 versus 25 of 280 (8.93 per cent), just over eight to one. The ordering the smoke test implied — that paying ₹49 predicted paying ₹499 far better than an email address — survived, on the correct bases. The test never established the market's absolute size.

Yatharth Fresh: the approach failed, and failed on inference

Yatharth Fresh, Gauhar Kamdar's Hyderabad fresh-produce venture, ran a textbook-looking test from 6 to 19 January 2025: 186,000 impressions, 5,580 clicks, 5,210 sessions, 4,880 unique visitors, 622 email signups — 622 of 4,880, or 12.75 per cent. Kamdar raised on it and committed ₹1.9 crore over seven months. The page promised ₹899 a month, farm-direct sourcing, next-morning delivery and free replacement of anything disliked.

It launched on 1 September 2025. Of the 622, 580 were reachable; 214 of 580 (36.9 per cent) started the free first box and 68 of 214 (31.8 per cent) paid for a second month, all 68 first paying in October 2025. At a 24.0 per cent gross margin, ₹899 yielded ₹215.76 of monthly contribution, so recovering the ₹2,980 acquisition cost needed 13.8 paying months. The chain gives two points on the survival curve and no curve: 38 of the 68 (55.9 per cent) still paid in their third paying month, December 2025, and 31 of the 68 (45.6 per cent) in their fifth, February 2026. Straight-line interpolation between those points crosses half the cohort at 4.1 paying months, worth ₹885 of contribution, or 0.30 times that cost. Lifetime value properly uses mean, not median, tenure; on roughly exponential decay the mean runs about 1.44 times the median, which would put it at 5.9 months and ₹1,273, or 0.43 times. Nor does the chain say whether the ₹2,980 was struck per paying subscriber or per box starter. On every reading lifetime value sat far below acquisition cost, and that is all the chain supports.

Nothing in the test's arithmetic was wrong; the inference was. A free email address given in response to free replacement and next-morning delivery measured appetite for a promise the economics could not keep, and the clause that lifted the signup rate later lifted returns and churn. A re-run from 9 to 22 March 2026 asked for a refundable ₹99 reservation instead: 41 of 3,110 unique visitors, or 1.32 per cent, took it — a rate on the same kind of base over a comparable fourteen-day window. But a paid reservation is not a free signup, and the creative and the season differed too, so the gap between 12.75 and 1.32 cannot be read as the price of the ask. Yatharth relaunched in June 2026 at ₹649, delivery charged separately and replacement limited to damaged items, lifting contribution to ₹177.83 a month against an acquisition cost of ₹1,410. Two paying months on, 118 of 173 relaunch payers (68.2 per cent) were still active in August 2026 — all 173 having first paid that June — against the launch cohort's 38 of the 68 at the same point: same measure, different cohorts, different offer. At ₹177.83 a month the relaunch recovers its ₹1,410 acquisition cost in 7.9 paying months, and four months in no cohort has reached that.

Yaksha Labs: real demand, for a product that did not exist yet

Gyanada Kolhatkar's Yaksha Labs built an agent that drafted GST reconciliation notes for chartered-accountant practices. From 11 to 31 August 2026 a landing page in three study-circle newsletters drew 2,420 unique visitors; 187 of 2,420 (7.73 per cent) requested access and 54 of 2,420 (2.23 per cent) uploaded a sample ledger — 54 of the 187 (28.9 per cent) who had asked. All 54 were drafted within 72 hours by two people behind the interface, ₹2,100 a ledger and ₹1,13,400 in all, and 38 of the 54 (70.4 per cent) were accepted without edits. Kolhatkar then had the same 54 re-run through the unassisted model, scored blind by the same reviewers on the same rubric: 11 of the 54 (20.4 per cent) passed. Ledgers, rubric and reviewers constant, the 50.0-point gap is like-for-like. The demand was real, and it was demand for the 70.4 per cent experience.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Base drift. Warning: the rate improves when someone rebuilds the dashboard. Question: what is the denominator, and when was it counted? Caught late, a build rests on an irreproducible figure.

Intent read as purchase. Warning: "conversion" in a sentence with no price in it. Question: what did the person give up? Yatharth's answer was nothing; the late cost was ₹1.9 crore.

Underpowered kill. Warning: a decision taken on fewer than forty events. Question: what difference could this sample detect? Caught late, the better idea is dead unnoticed.

Over-promised page. Warning: compliance asks for a change the team resists, or the cost per click sits far below the category norm. Question: can we ship this sentence, and would we sell to these people at full price? Caught late, the churn reads as a product problem.

Escalation of commitment. Warning: the sponsor presents the rate before the base. Question: what rate, written in advance, would have killed this? Caught late, the build grows a constituency.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a free-signup rate transfer at all? The commitment school says no: the rate is a function of the ask's cost, so only costly asks may be projected. Its best evidence is Yuvasetu's eight-to-one cohort gap, measured inside one company at one launch. Yatharth's 12.75 per cent against 1.32 per cent once money entered points the same way, but confounds ask, creative and window and compares absolute levels across companies, so it cannot carry the claim. Demand-first says yes, relatively: hold page, channel and ask constant and the differences between arms are informative even though the levels are not, a claim resting on a hundred years of split-run mail. The first position would be wrong if a corpus showed stable free-to-paid ratios within a category; the second, if arm orderings flipped when the ask's cost changed. Nobody has run that study at scale.

Should a smoke test ever run on an audience you own? For: nearly free, fast, the only option without a media budget. Against: a biased sample, trust spent that belongs to the next test, an answer about retention rather than acquisition. Both agree the owned-audience rate must never sit beside a bought-traffic rate; they disagree about collecting it.

Is an underpowered test worse than none? The research-design school says yes: a confident wrong answer costs more than acknowledged ignorance. Pragmatists answer with an asymmetry: at n of several thousand a near-zero rate is hard to produce by noise, while a high rate has many benign explanations, so a short test is legitimate for stopping and illegitimate for starting. Nor is the AI-native variant settled: whether Yaksha Labs's measurement was valuable or dangerous turns on whether the organisation can hold the quality distinction.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs a page and reports a percentage. Someone who has internalised it writes the decision and the kill threshold down before buying a single impression, names the base and its counting date in every sentence containing a rate, is more interested in the 37 than the 361, and declines the test when the binding risk is not demand. The clearest tell comes before the test: such a practitioner can say in advance what result would stop the project.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Kanitkar committed ₹62 lakh rather than ₹2.4 crore: the 5.07 per cent signup rate justified further investigation and nothing more, because the only purchase-adjacent cell held 37 observations and a decision-grade reservation comparison needed about fifteen thousand visitors an arm.

Kelshikar declined the landing page and spent ₹2.1 lakh on an account-based test from 4 May to 29 June 2026. Gulika Kotecha's team contacted 96 named accounts, reached 71 of 96 decision-makers (74.0 per cent), held spec reviews with 23 of 71 (32.4 per cent), took non-binding letters of intent from 9 of 71 (12.7 per cent), and sold four paid 60-day pilots at ₹1.5 lakh each — ₹6.0 lakh of cash, from 4 of 96 accounts contacted (4.2 per cent). Three pilots became annual contracts worth ₹18 lakh each, signed 18 September 2026. Kotecha's first board draft called this proof that account-based testing beats landing pages. Kelshikar struck the sentence: the landing page was never run, so the two methods were never applied to one population. What the account test showed was that this market yields usable counts when approached by name; Exhibit 6, computed beforehand on a category benchmark, separately shows why a landing page here would be low-resolution. Neither ranks the methods.

For discussion. (1) Kanitkar wrote no threshold before the test. Had he written one, what rate — on which base — should have stopped Interview Coach? (2) Yatharth's page was truthful about an offer it could not sustain. Where does responsibility sit: the test design, the pricing, or treating a signup rate as a demand estimate? (3) Yaksha Labs measured real demand for a quality it reached only with people in the loop at ₹2,100 a ledger. Is that a validated business, a validated service business, or neither?

13. Going deeper

  • Designing discovery experiments — the threshold-before-test habit Kanitkar lacked.
  • MVP types — what you build once the smoke clears.
  • The four product risks — whether a demand test addresses the binding risk at all.
  • Fake doors and painted doors — the in-product variant and its trust cost.
  • Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests — how Yaksha Labs drafted 54 notes with no system.
  • Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits — Exhibit 5's upper rungs, the enterprise instruments.
  • Prototype testing — what to do with the list a test produces.
  • The evidence ladder — which evidence earns which decision.
